newsitem.title: ITALY: Serbian opposition says Milosevic's days numbered.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition says Milosevic's days numbered.

text.p: Opposition leader Vuk Draskovic said on Friday he believed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic would be out of power by the end of the year and urged the West to raise the pressure on him to reinstate annulled elections.

"I am quite sure this is the last year of Milosevic's rule in Serbia," Draskovic said in Rome, where he and co-leaders of the Zajedno (Together) coalition met Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini for talks on the crisis.
"Very many people are against Milosevic. The majority of people are against Milosevic," he told Reuters Television.
Zajedno has staged 60 days of protests on the streets of Belgrade to try to force Milosevic and his Socialist Party (SPS) to recognise opposition victories in local polls on November 17.
Their protests are the biggest challenge to the 10-year rule of Milosevic, who called on Thursday for economic reforms in Serbia but maintained his silence on the vote fraud.
Zajedno says it will step up protests by blockading traffic and public institutions if Milosevic refuses to give way.
"We can't just wait forever till he changes his mind," co-leader Vesna Pesic told a news conference after meeting Dini.
Asked for more details, Draskovic said only that the fresh protests would be peaceful. "I prefer to surprise you," he said.
The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) told Milosevic on Thursday to respect opposition victories and stop trying to solve the crisis by piecemeal concessions.
The European Parliament also passed a resolution saying the European Union and its individual member states should freeze relations with Serbia until democracy was established there.
Pesic said the crisis would be discussed by EU foreign ministers on Monday, but Draskovic was unimpressed by international action so far.
"I am not quite satisified with international pressure because that pressure is not very effective," he said.

He said it was the duty of the major powers which obtained Milosevic's signature to the 1995 Dayton accords that ended the war in Bosnia to make sure he respected the commitments made in the agreement to fostering democracy in the region.

"I am not an adviser to the United States government or the European Union but they must find a real and effective way to force Milosevic to respect (the election results and Dayton)," he told the news conference.
Draskovic said recognition of the election results was the "condition of all conditions" but stopped short of calling for a resumption of international economic sanctions against Serbia.

"Against Milosevic and his Mafia, yes. Not against our state and people because the people are suffering too much. The biggest sanction...against Serbia is Mr Milosevic and his dictatorship," Draskovic said.
Electoral commissions in Belgrade and Nis, Serbia's second city, have ordered the opposition victories restored, but Socialist hardliners say they will challenge this.
Dini claimed credit last month for obtaining an undertaking from Milosevic to allow an OSCE mission to visit Serbia and investigate the polls. It found the opposition won.
Dini, however, angered Zajedno during the same visit when he said reinstatement of the disputed election results was not "on the cards" as a basis for dialogue with Milosevic.
Draskovic said the row had been resolved. "I like misunderstandings finishing as understandings," he said.
